# The Question {.divider background-color="#3498db"}

[Act I]{.act}

## Does health insurance actually make people healthier?

The U.S. spends more on health care than any other rich country — yet millions of adults have no
insurance.

. . .

If we gave them coverage, would their **health** improve, or only their **health-care bills**?

::: {.notes}
Open with the policy stakes. Insurance debates (e.g., the Affordable Care Act) turn on this exact
question. Ask the room for a show of hands: who thinks insurance improves health? Keep their answers
in mind — we will test the intuition against two real experiments.
:::

## In survey data, insured adults report better health

| Group | Average health (1 = poor, 5 = excellent) |
|:---|---:|
| Uninsured | 3.66 |
| Insured | [3.98]{.key} |

[National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) 2009 — married adults aged 26–59, $n = 18{,}790$.]{.comment}

[The insured look healthier. The question is whether insurance *caused* the gap.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the first, most natural piece of evidence anyone would look at. A gap of about 0.3 points on
a 5-point scale is sizeable. Before celebrating, ask: who chooses to have insurance? That question
drives the rest of the lecture.
:::

## Three lines of pandas reproduce the naive comparison

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7"}
import pandas as pd                       # pandas → load and summarize tables

# every course dataset lives in the repo's data/ folder on GitHub
GITHUB_DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cmg777/intro2causal/main/data/"
nhis = pd.read_csv(GITHUB_DATA_URL + "ch1/nhis_clean.csv")   # NHIS 2009 extract

nhis.groupby("insurance")["health"].mean()   # mean health: 0 = uninsured, 1 = insured
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
`groupby("insurance")` splits the sample into insured and uninsured; `["health"].mean()` averages
the 1–5 health index in each group. Output: 3.66 for the uninsured, 3.98 for the insured.
The data file is already cleaned — see code/python/ch1/prepare_data.py for how.
:::

## Our route through the chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **The question** — why a simple comparison cannot settle cause and effect
- **The investigation** — potential outcomes, selection bias, and regression on a dummy; why random
  assignment removes the bias; two landmark insurance experiments (RAND and Oregon)
- **The resolution** — what the experiments teach, how to read standard errors, and the traps to avoid
:::

::: {.notes}
Learning objectives: explain why naive comparisons fail; define potential outcomes, selection bias,
average treatment effects; describe how random assignment eliminates selection bias; use regression
on a dummy to compare means; interpret the RAND and Oregon experiments; understand standard errors
and statistical significance.
:::

## Three ideas carry the whole chapter

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Potential outcomes
Each person has a health level **with** insurance ($Y_{1i}$) and **without** it ($Y_{0i}$).
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Selection bias
People who choose treatment differ from those who don't — *before* any treatment.
:::
::: {.column width="34%"}
### Random assignment
A lottery decides who is treated, so the groups are alike on average.
:::
::::

[The chapter is the story of how the third idea solves the problem the first two reveal.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Other vocabulary we will meet along the way: causal effect, confounder, balance check, standard
error, t-statistic, statistical significance, moral hazard, intent-to-treat, clustered standard
errors. Define them as they come up rather than all at once.
:::

# The Investigation {.divider background-color="#8e44ad"}

[Act II]{.act}

## Every person has two potential outcomes, but we only ever see one

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The two roads
- $Y_{1i}$ — person $i$'s health **with** insurance
- $Y_{0i}$ — the same person's health **without** it
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The causal effect
$$Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$$
Only one road is ever travelled, so one term is always missing.
:::
::::

[A causal effect compares a person with *themselves* in another world — not with someone else.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Fork-in-the-road picture: you take one path and never learn where the other would have led. The
unobserved outcome is called the counterfactual.
:::

## A naive comparison can even get the sign wrong

| | Anika | Ben |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Health without insurance ($Y_{0i}$) | 3 | 5 |
| Health with insurance ($Y_{1i}$) | 4 | 5 |
| Buys insurance? ($D_i$) | Yes | No |
| **Observed health** | 4 | 5 |
| True effect | [+1]{.key} | 0 |

[Insured Anika (4) looks *worse* than uninsured Ben (5), yet insurance helped her by +1.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Two hypothetical students. Anika is prone to illness and buys insurance; Ben is naturally robust and
skips it. Naive comparison: 4 − 5 = −1, suggesting insurance harms health. The truth for Anika is +1.
The comparison is polluted by the fact that Ben started out healthier.
:::

## Any observed gap = causal effect + selection bias

$$\text{Observed difference} \;=\; \kappa \;+\; \text{Selection bias}$$

. . .

$$\text{Selection bias} \;=\; \text{Avg}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i=1] \;-\; \text{Avg}[Y_{0i} \mid D_i=0]$$

[The health gap that would exist between the two groups *even if nobody had insurance*.]{.comment}

[Unless the bias term is zero, the observed gap does not equal the causal effect $\kappa$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
κ (kappa) is the causal effect of insurance, assumed the same for everyone for simplicity. The
selection-bias term compares the no-insurance health of people who did buy insurance with the
no-insurance health of people who did not. In the NHIS, healthier, richer, better-educated people
are more likely to be insured, so this term is likely positive.
:::

## Confounders open a back-door path from insurance to health

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    C["Confounders: education, income"] -->|"affects"| I["Insurance status"]
    C -->|"affects"| H["Health"]
    I -.->|"causal effect?"| H
    style C fill:#e67e22,color:#fff
    style I fill:#3498db,color:#fff
    style H fill:#2d8659,color:#fff
```

[Because the same traits drive both insurance and health, the raw gap mixes their influence with any true effect.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A confounder is a variable that influences both treatment and outcome. The dashed arrow is what we
want to measure; the solid arrows through the confounders are what contaminate the comparison.
:::

## We can never observe both roads for the same person

The individual effect $Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$ is **unobservable** — this is the *fundamental problem of
causal inference*.

. . .

We cannot fix it with more data on the same people. We need a **research design** that makes the
selection-bias term disappear.

[Causal inference is the art of building a believable stand-in for the road not taken.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Every method in this course — randomized trials, regression, IV, RD, differences-in-differences — is
a different strategy for constructing a credible counterfactual.
:::

## Regressing an outcome on a dummy reproduces the difference in means

$$Y_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + e_i$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- $\alpha$ (intercept) = average $Y$ when $D_i = 0$
- $\beta$ (slope) = treated mean − control mean
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- $D_i$ is a **dummy**: 1 = insured, 0 = uninsured
- In code: `health ~ insurance`
:::
::::

[Regression on a dummy is just a comparison of means — plus a standard error for free.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Here Y is the health index (`health`) and D is the insurance dummy (`insurance`). The coefficient on
the dummy is exactly the gap between group averages; regression adds a measure of precision.
:::

## A standard error tells us whether a gap is bigger than noise

- **Standard error (SE):** how much an estimate would wobble across different samples
- **t-statistic** = coefficient ÷ SE
- **Rule of thumb:** $|t| > 2$ → statistically significant at the 5% level

. . .

| Purpose of the regression | What we hope to see |
|:---|:---|
| Balance check | **small** $t$ — groups look alike |
| Treatment effect | **large** $t$ — evidence of an effect |

[Read every coefficient together with its standard error.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Bathroom-scale analogy: a good scale gives consistent readings (small SE), a cheap one jumps around
(large SE). Throughout the chapter, standard errors appear in parentheses next to coefficients.
:::

## One `pf.feols` call gives the gap and its standard error

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7|9-11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                  # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab

import pandas as pd                       # pandas → load tables
import pyfixest as pf                     # pyfixest → regressions with robust SEs

GITHUB_DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cmg777/intro2causal/main/data/"
nhis = pd.read_csv(GITHUB_DATA_URL + "ch1/nhis_clean.csv")   # NHIS 2009 extract

# health on the insurance dummy, with survey weights and robust (hetero) SEs
m = pf.feols("health ~ insurance", data=nhis, weights="weight", vcov="hetero")
m.summary()                               # Intercept 3.66 = uninsured; insurance 0.35 (0.02)
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
`weights="weight"` applies the survey weights so the sample represents the population.
`vcov="hetero"` asks for heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Swap `health` for `education`
or `family_income` to reproduce each row of the next table.
:::

## The insured differ from the uninsured on almost everything

::: {.small-table}
| Characteristic | Uninsured mean | Insured − uninsured (SE) |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Health index (1–5) | 3.66 | 0.35 (0.02) |
| Nonwhite (share) | 0.17 | −0.02 (0.01) |
| Age (years) | 40.51 | 2.61 (0.21) |
| Education (years) | 11.67 | [2.70 (0.07)]{.key} |
| Family size | 3.95 | −0.45 (0.04) |
| Employed (share) | 0.72 | 0.13 (0.01) |
| Family income (\$) | 45,989 | [60,352 (976)]{.key} |
:::

[Insured adults are older, ~3 years more educated, and \$60,000 richer — red flags for selection bias.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Each row is a separate weighted regression of the characteristic on the insurance dummy, with robust
standard errors. Nearly every gap is many standard errors from zero. The health gap is almost
certainly driven, at least in part, by these pre-existing advantages.
:::

## A coin flip breaks the link between treatment and personal traits

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    P["Target population"] --> R["Random assignment"]
    R -->|"heads"| T["Treated: insured"]
    R -->|"tails"| C["Control: uninsured"]
    T --> D["Gap in means = causal effect"]
    C --> D
    style P fill:#3498db,color:#fff
    style R fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff
    style T fill:#2d8659,color:#fff
    style C fill:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style D fill:#2d8659,color:#fff
```

[When a lottery — not the person — decides who is treated, choice can no longer bias the comparison.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A randomized controlled trial (RCT) draws both groups from the same population. Education, income,
health habits — and traits we cannot even measure — have no say in who gets treated.
:::

## With enough people, randomization balances even what we cannot measure

- Roll a die 10 times: the average may be far from 3.5
- Roll it 10,000 times: the average is almost exactly 3.5

. . .

The **law of large numbers** does the same for randomized groups: their averages converge to the
population average — for age, income, motivation, genes, *everything*.

[Large randomized groups are alike on observed **and** unobserved traits.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Casino analogy: any single bet is a toss-up, but over thousands of plays the house edge always wins.
The same averaging makes treatment and control groups comparable. With small samples, chance
imbalances remain possible — another reason to check balance.
:::

## Under random assignment the selection-bias term vanishes

$$E[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 1] = E[Y_{0i} \mid D_i = 0]$$

. . .

$$\Rightarrow\quad E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = \kappa$$

[Randomization makes the simple difference in means an unbiased estimate of the causal effect.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
First line: with random assignment, the treated and control groups would have had the same average
health without treatment. Plug that into the decomposition: the selection-bias term is zero, so the
observed difference equals κ.
:::

## Controlled comparisons have a long history

::: {.small-table}
| When | Who | Contribution |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1747 | James Lind | Compared scurvy remedies on sailors — citrus worked |
| 1885 | Peirce & Jastrow | First deliberate **random** assignment |
| 1925 | R. A. Fisher | Formalized randomized experimental design |
| 1974 | RAND | The largest social experiment of its era |
:::

[Randomization went from a statistician's idea to the gold standard for policy evaluation.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Lind's theory (acids cure scurvy) was wrong, but his data were right — a lesson in letting evidence
speak. An even older story describes a ten-day diet trial with a comparison group around 600 BCE.
:::

## RAND randomized ~4,000 people across insurance plans of different generosity

| Plan | Participants pay | Role |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Catastrophic | ~95% of costs (capped) | **Control** (≈ no insurance) |
| Deductible | 95% of outpatient costs | Moderate treatment |
| Coinsurance | 25–50% of costs | Moderate treatment |
| Free | Nothing | [Most generous treatment]{.key} |

[Two questions: does cheaper care raise use — and does more care improve health?]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The RAND Health Insurance Experiment ran from 1974 to 1982 at six U.S. sites. Families, not
individuals, were randomized to plans. The catastrophic plan is the omitted reference group in every
regression that follows.
:::

## Before the experiment, plan groups looked alike

::: {.small-table}
| Baseline trait | Catastrophic mean | Free − Cat. | Deductible − Cat. | Coinsurance − Cat. |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Female (share) | 0.56 | −0.04 (0.01) | −0.02 (0.02) | −0.02 (0.02) |
| Age (years) | 32.4 | 0.43 (0.61) | 0.56 (0.68) | 0.97 (0.65) |
| Education (years) | 12.1 | −0.26 (0.18) | −0.16 (0.19) | −0.06 (0.19) |
| Family income (\$) | 31,603 | −976 (1,345) | −2,104 (1,384) | 970 (1,389) |
| Health index | 70.9 | −1.31 (0.87) | −1.44 (0.95) | 0.21 (0.92) |
| Mental health | 73.9 | 0.89 (0.77) | −0.12 (0.82) | 1.19 (0.81) |
:::

[Gaps are small, point in both directions, and are mostly insignificant — randomization worked.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Each row regresses a baseline trait on the three plan dummies, clustering standard errors by family
because whole families shared a plan. Contrast with the NHIS table, where every gap was huge.
Not shown: nonwhite, cholesterol, and blood pressure — also balanced. With many comparisons, one or
two "significant" gaps (like female) are expected by chance.
:::

## A balance check is the same regression, run on a baseline trait

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-6|8-10|11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                  # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                       # pandas → load tables
import pyfixest as pf                     # pyfixest → regressions with clustered SEs

GITHUB_DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cmg777/intro2causal/main/data/"
rand = pd.read_csv(GITHUB_DATA_URL + "ch1/rand_balance.csv")   # RAND baseline traits

# age on plan dummies; the catastrophic plan is the omitted control group
m = pf.feols("age ~ plan_free + plan_deductible + plan_coinsurance",
             data=rand, vcov={"CRV1": "family_id"})   # cluster SEs by family
m.summary()                               # Intercept 32.4; plan gaps 0.4–1.0, all |t| < 2
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
`vcov={"CRV1": "family_id"}` clusters standard errors by family: family members share a plan, so
their outcomes are not independent, and ignoring that would overstate precision. pyfixest drops rows
with missing values in the model variables automatically. Swap `age` for any baseline trait.
:::

## Free care raised doctor visits and spending sharply

::: {.small-table}
| Use per person-year | Catastrophic mean | Free effect (SE) | Deductible effect | Coinsurance effect |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Doctor visits | 2.78 | [+1.66 (0.25)]{.key} | +0.19 (0.25) | +0.48 (0.24) |
| Outpatient spending (\$) | 248 | +169 (20) | +42 (21) | +60 (21) |
| Hospital admissions | 0.10 | +0.03 (0.01) | +0.02 (0.01) | +0.00 (0.01) |
| Total spending (\$) | 636 | [+285 (72)]{.key} | +114 (79) | +152 (84) |
:::

[When care became free, people used much more of it — the demand curve at work.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Because plans were randomly assigned, these coefficients are causal effects relative to the
catastrophic plan. Outpatient spending rose 68% (169 / 248). Inpatient spending (not shown): +116
(60) on the free plan. Spending is in inflation-adjusted dollars.
:::

## Total spending: free plan vs catastrophic plan {background-color="#8e44ad"}

[+45%]{.bignum}

[more health spending when care was free (+\$285 on a \$636 base)]{.bignum-label}

::: {.notes}
285 / 636 ≈ 45%. Economists call this response moral hazard — not a moral judgment, just the
observation that people consume more of something when its price at the point of use falls to zero.
:::

## Estimating a causal effect uses exactly the same call

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-6|8-10|11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                  # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                       # pandas → load tables
import pyfixest as pf                     # pyfixest → regressions with clustered SEs

GITHUB_DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cmg777/intro2causal/main/data/"
hie = pd.read_csv(GITHUB_DATA_URL + "ch1/rand_utilization.csv")   # person-year use data

# total spending on plan dummies — causal, because plans were randomized
m = pf.feols("total_expenses ~ plan_free + plan_deductible + plan_coinsurance",
             data=hie, vcov={"CRV1": "family_id"})    # cluster SEs by family
m.summary()                               # Intercept 636; plan_free +285 (SE 72)
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Same formula as the balance check, different left-hand variable. Before randomization we *hope* for
small coefficients (balance); after, large coefficients are evidence of causal effects. Try `visits`
or `outpatient_expenses` in place of `total_expenses`.
:::

## Yet health at the end was no better on the free plan

::: {.small-table}
| Exit health measure | Catastrophic mean | Free effect (SE) | Deductible effect | Coinsurance effect |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| General health index | 68.5 | −0.78 (0.87) | −0.87 (0.96) | 0.61 (0.90) |
| Cholesterol | 203.2 | −1.83 (2.39) | 0.69 (2.57) | −2.31 (2.47) |
| Blood pressure | 121.9 | −0.52 (0.93) | 1.17 (1.06) | −1.39 (0.98) |
| Mental health index | 75.5 | 0.43 (0.82) | 0.45 (0.91) | 1.07 (0.87) |
:::

[45% more care bought no measurable improvement in health.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These outcomes were measured 3–5 years after random assignment. Every effect is small relative to
the control mean and statistically insignificant. This is the RAND paradox: more care, not more
health.
:::

## The null is precise: the data rule out large health gains

Free-plan effect on the general health index: $-0.78$ with SE $0.87$

. . .

95% confidence interval $\approx -0.78 \pm 2 \times 0.87 = [-2.5,\ 1.0]$ — on a control mean of 68.5

[The experiment was big enough to find a meaningful effect; the effect simply wasn't there.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A "precisely estimated null" differs from an underpowered study. Even the most optimistic end of the
interval (+1.0 point on a ~68-point scale) is a tiny health gain. Lessons from RAND: people respond
to prices; more care does not automatically mean better health; randomization exposed the NHIS gap
as mostly selection bias.
:::

## Oregon's 2008 lottery tested insurance for low-income adults

- RAND studied **middle-class families** who all had at least catastrophic coverage
- Oregon: about **75,000** low-income, uninsured adults applied to expanded Medicaid
- About **30,000** were drawn by lottery to apply for coverage

[A lottery for a public program created a new randomized experiment — for the people today's debates are about.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Studied by Amy Finkelstein, Katherine Baicker and colleagues (2012, 2013). Today's uninsured are
younger, poorer and less educated than the RAND participants — would insurance help them more?
:::

## Only a quarter of winners enrolled, so we first measure intent-to-treat

- **Intent-to-treat (ITT):** the effect of *winning the lottery*, whether or not the winner enrolled
- Winning raised Medicaid enrollment by about **25.6 percentage points**

. . .

$$\text{effect of insurance on enrollees} \approx \frac{\text{ITT}}{\text{effect of winning on enrollment}}$$

[Scaling the ITT by the enrollment jump previews instrumental variables (Chapter 3).]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Many winners failed to complete paperwork or turned out to be ineligible. Comparing winners with
losers is still a clean randomized comparison — it just measures the effect of the *offer*. Dividing
by the change in enrollment converts it into the effect of insurance itself.
:::

## Winning improved finances and mental health, not physical health

::: {.small-table}
| Outcome | Effect of winning the lottery |
|:---|:---|
| Medicaid enrollment | +25.6 percentage points |
| Emergency-department visits | +10% (a *decrease* was expected) |
| Self-reported health | Modest improvement (+3.9 pp) |
| Physical health (cholesterol, blood pressure) | [No significant change]{.key} |
| Mental health | Improved |
| Catastrophic expenses and medical debt | Decreased |
:::

[Insurance protected wallets and moods; it did not move clinical measures.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Results from Finkelstein et al. (2012) and Baicker et al. (2013). Note the surprise on emergency
visits: some policymakers expected coverage to shift care away from the ER; instead ER use rose.
:::

## Two experiments, decades apart, agree on physical health

| | RAND (1974–1982) | Oregon (2008) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Population | Middle-class families | Low-income adults |
| More care used? | Yes | Yes |
| Better physical health? | [No]{.key} | [No]{.key} |
| Better mental health? | Not measured | Yes |
| Less financial hardship? | Not measured | Yes |

[Insurance's clearest benefits may be financial protection and peace of mind.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Two very different populations, two different eras, the same physical-health finding. Oregon added
the financial-protection and mental-health results.
:::

## Standard errors and confidence intervals measure sampling noise

::: {.small-table}
| Tool | Symbol | Plain meaning |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| Sample mean | $\bar{Y}$ | The average in our data |
| Standard error | $SE(\bar{Y})$ | How much $\bar{Y}$ would vary across samples |
| t-statistic | coef / SE | How many SEs the estimate is from zero |
| 95% confidence interval | estimate $\pm 2 \times SE$ | Values consistent with the data |
:::

[Any estimate from a sample would change with a new sample — inference quantifies by how much.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the toolkit we used implicitly all chapter: SEs in parentheses, |t| > 2 for significance,
and the ±2 SE interval we used to show RAND's null was precise.
:::

## Significance measures precision, not importance

- A huge sample can make a **tiny** effect "significant"
- A small sample can leave a **large** effect "insignificant"
- **Not significant ≠ no effect** — it may just mean too little data

[Always report the size of a coefficient *and* its precision.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Fire-alarm analogy: significance tells you the alarm went off, not how big the fire is. Look at the
magnitude relative to a meaningful benchmark (e.g., the control mean) as well as the t-statistic.
:::

# The Resolution {.divider background-color="#2d8659"}

[Act III]{.act}

## The tempting mistake: "The insured are healthier, so insurance works"

[Objection.]{.objection} Insured adults report better health, so coverage must improve health.

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} The gap bundles any causal effect with selection bias — the insured were
already older, richer and better educated. When RAND randomized coverage, the health advantage
disappeared.

::: {.notes}
This is correlation-versus-causation in its most policy-relevant form. Recall the Anika/Ben example:
the naive gap can even have the wrong sign.
:::

## The tempting mistake: "Not significant means no effect"

[Objection.]{.objection} RAND's health effects are insignificant, so maybe the study was just too small.

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} Only if the estimate is imprecise. RAND's confidence intervals are narrow and
exclude large gains — a *precisely estimated* null, not a failure to look.

::: {.notes}
The distinction between "we found no effect" and "we found evidence of no large effect" is one of the
most important habits in empirical work.
:::

## Key takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- Any comparison of groups = **causal effect + selection bias**
- **Random assignment** sets selection bias to zero — then **check balance**
- **Regression on a dummy** = difference in means + a standard error
- **RAND:** free care raised spending 45% but did not improve health
- **Oregon:** insurance brought financial protection and better mental health
:::

::: {.notes}
Tie back to the opening show of hands: the intuition that insurance improves health is not wrong in
every sense — it protects finances and mental health — but the physical-health effect in these
experiments was small.
:::
